H1.text: A kite tugs on its string. A swing hangs from two ropes. A team leans back in a tug of war.

H2.text: Each time, a rope is pulling. And that pull can change, even when the load does not.

H3.text: At her grandmother's village, Diya pulls a bucket of water up from the well.

H4.text: Holding it still is easy. But when she starts to pull it up faster, the rope feels heavier. The water did not change.

H5.text: So what is the rope really doing? The answer is tension.

P2.text: When a rope is pulled tight, it pulls on whatever is tied to it. That pull is the tension, T.

P3.text: Tension always points along the rope, away from the body. A rope can pull, but it can never push.

P4.text: For a light rope, with almost no mass, the tension is the same all along it.

P5.text: A smooth pulley only turns the rope. So Diya's pull is the same as the pull on the bucket.

S1.text: To the motion notebook. A five kilogram bucket hangs on the rope.

S2.text: Its weight, m g, is forty nine newtons. Hanging still, the rope pulls up with exactly forty nine.

S3.text: Now Diya pulls it up faster and faster. The acceleration is two metres per second squared, upward.

S4.text: Slow-mo replay. Freeze, and draw the forces.

S5.text: T is now fifty nine newtons. It beats the weight by ten, and those ten newtons speed the bucket up.

S6.text: Let it run. Now it rises at a steady speed. a is zero, so T falls back to forty nine.

S7.text: Near the top, she lets it slow down. a points down, and T drops to thirty nine.

S8.text: On the graph, T moves along a straight line. Each unit of upward acceleration adds five newtons.

S9.text: Your turn. The bucket rises at a steady one metre per second. Is T bigger than m g, or equal? Pause and decide.

S10.text: Equal! Steady speed means no acceleration. So the forces balance, and T equals m g.

D1.text: Now let's write it down, one step at a time.

D2.text: Step one. Two forces act on the bucket. T pulls up, and m g pulls down.

D3.text: Step two. Take up as positive. The net force is T minus m g. By the second law, that equals m a.

D4.text: Step three. Move m g across. T equals m g plus m a. That is, T equals m times g plus a.

D5.text: Step four. Hanging still, or moving at a steady speed, a is zero. So T equals m g.

D6.text: Step five. If a points down, a is negative. Then T equals m times g minus a.

T1.text: Remember this. Tension follows the acceleration, not the direction of motion.

K1.text: Side by side. On the left, the bucket is pulled up faster and faster. a points up, so T is m times g plus a. Fifty nine newtons.

K2.text: On the right, it is lowered faster and faster. a points down, so T is m times g minus a. Thirty nine.

K3.text: Now you try. The bucket is still rising, but slowing down. Is T more or less than m g? Pause and decide.

K4.text: Less! It is slowing while moving up, so a points down. Then T is m times g minus a.

W2.text: The five kilogram bucket is pulled up at two metres per second squared, over a smooth pulley. How hard must Diya pull? g is nine point eight.

W3.text: a points up, so T equals m times g plus a.

W4.text: That is five times nine point eight plus two. Five times eleven point eight. Fifty nine newtons.

W5.text: The rope is light and the pulley is smooth, so the tension is the same all along. Diya pulls with fifty nine newtons.

W6.text: Ten newtons more than the bucket's weight. That is why starting the pull feels heavier.

X2.text: Many students say: the bucket moves up, so T must be bigger than m g.

X3.text: But only the acceleration counts. At a steady speed, T equals m g. Rising and slowing, T is less than m g.

E1.text: Where is this asked? In free-body numericals: bodies hanging on strings, and ropes that can break.

Q1.text: Exam level now. A rope breaks above three hundred newtons. It is used to lower a forty kilogram sack. g is ten. What acceleration keeps the rope safe? Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is A. At least two point five metres per second squared, downward.

A2.text: The weight is four hundred newtons, more than three hundred. So the rope cannot hold the sack still.

A3.text: Going down, T equals m times g minus a. Forty times ten minus a must be at most three hundred.

A4.text: So ten minus a is at most seven point five. a is at least two point five, downward.

Y3.text: Two. Why is the tension the same all along a light rope?
